outline.chapter_title: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models
outline.description: This chapter sets the stage by introducing the role of reinforcement learning in scaling large language models. It covers the motivation behind RL training, the types of tasks it enables (e.g., competition-level math and programming), and provides a high-level overview of the stability challenges that current algorithms face, motivating the need for a new approach like GSPO.
subtopics: The role of reinforcement learning in advancing language model capabilities
Deep reasoning and long-form generation tasks enabled by large-scale RL
Stability challenges in training gigantic language models with RL
Model collapse: causes, consequences, and irreversibility
Overview of GSPO as a solution: sequence-level optimization for stable training
The contributions of GSPO to the Qwen3 model family

outline.description: This chapter provides the necessary background on the two predecessor algorithms that GSPO builds upon and improves: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). It covers the mathematical formulations, key mechanisms (clipping, importance ratios, advantage estimation), and the practical limitations of each algorithm that motivated the development of GSPO.
subtopics: Notation and preliminaries: policies, queries, responses, rewards, and verifiers
Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO): objective function and clipping mechanism
Token-level importance ratios in PPO: definition and role
Value models in PPO: purpose, computational burden, and scalability challenges
Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO): eliminating the value model
Group-based advantage estimation: normalizing rewards across multiple responses
Shared advantage across tokens in GRPO
Practical limitations of PPO and GRPO: memory, computational overhead, and stability

outline.chapter_title: The Instability Problem: Why GRPO's Objective is Ill-Posed
outline.description: This chapter provides a deep theoretical analysis of the fundamental flaw in GRPO's design. It introduces the principle of importance sampling, explains why applying importance weights at the token level violates this principle, and demonstrates how this misapplication introduces high-variance noise that accumulates over long sequences and is exacerbated by clipping, ultimately leading to model collapse.
subtopics: Off-policy learning in RL: mini-batch gradient updates and distributional mismatch
The principle of importance sampling: correct usage and requirements
Importance sampling formulation: target vs. behavior distributions and the role of multiple samples
GRPO's misapplication: token-level importance weights from single samples
Why token-level importance weights fail to perform distribution correction
Accumulation of high-variance noise over long sequences
How the clipping mechanism amplifies the instability
Empirical observations of catastrophic and irreversible model collapse
The core principle: matching the unit of optimization to the unit of reward

outline.description: This chapter presents the core contribution of the paper: the Group Sequence Policy Optimization algorithm. It defines the sequence-level importance ratio, explains its theoretical grounding, presents the GSPO objective function with sequence-level clipping, and provides a detailed gradient analysis comparing GSPO with GRPO to illuminate the fundamental difference in how each algorithm weights token-level gradients.
subtopics: Sequence-level importance ratio: definition and theoretical meaning
Length normalization in the importance ratio: motivation and benefits for variance reduction
The GSPO objective function: sequence-level clipping and group-based advantages
Clipping at the sequence level vs. token level: conceptual differences
Differences in clipping range magnitudes between GSPO and GRPO
Gradient analysis of GSPO: deriving the gradient of the sequence-level objective
Gradient analysis of GRPO: deriving the gradient for comparison
Key insight: equal vs. unequal weighting of token gradients in GSPO and GRPO
How GSPO eliminates the instability factor of unequal token weights

outline.description: This chapter introduces GSPO-token, a variant of GSPO designed for scenarios requiring finer-grained advantage adjustment at the token level, such as multi-turn RL. It presents the mathematical formulation using stop-gradient operations, derives the gradient, and demonstrates that GSPO-token is numerically identical to GSPO when token advantages are uniform, while offering additional flexibility for per-token advantage customization.
subtopics: Motivation for token-level advantage adjustment: multi-turn RL scenarios
Formulation of GSPO-token: incorporating stop-gradient operations
The role of stop-gradient (detach) in maintaining numerical equivalence
Derivation of the GSPO-token gradient
Numerical equivalence between GSPO-token and GSPO under uniform advantages
Flexibility of GSPO-token for per-token advantage customization
Practical use cases: when to use GSPO vs. GSPO-token

outline.description: This chapter presents the experimental results demonstrating GSPO's superiority over GRPO. It covers the training setup, benchmarks used, and key findings including training stability, efficiency gains, and a counter-intuitive observation about clipping fractions that provides further evidence of GRPO's inherent noise and GSPO's more effective learning signal.
subtopics: Experimental setup: cold-start model, training configuration, and benchmarks (AIME'24, LiveCodeBench, CodeForces)
Mini-batch partitioning and clipping range settings for fair comparison
Training reward curves: stability and convergence comparison
Benchmark performance: Pass@1 and Elo Rating comparisons
Training efficiency: GSPO's superior performance under equal compute and query consumption
The clipping fraction observation: two orders of magnitude difference between GSPO and GRPO
Counter-intuitive finding: more clipping leads to better efficiency
Evidence that GRPO's token-level gradient estimates are inherently noisy
GSPO's role in the RL training of the Qwen3 models

outline.description: This chapter addresses the unique stability challenges that arise when applying RL to Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. It explains the expert-activation volatility problem, describes the Routing Replay workaround previously needed for GRPO, and shows how GSPO fundamentally resolves this issue by focusing on sequence likelihood rather than individual token likelihoods, thereby simplifying the training process.
subtopics: Background on Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models and sparse activation
Expert-activation volatility: how gradient updates change activated experts
Quantifying expert volatility: ~10% expert change per update in Qwen3-30B-A3B
How expert volatility invalidates token-level importance ratios in GRPO
Routing Replay: caching and replaying expert routing modes across updates
Limitations of Routing Replay: memory, communication overhead, and reduced model capacity
How GSPO resolves expert-activation volatility: insensitivity to individual token likelihoods
Sequence likelihood stability in MoE models despite routing changes
Elimination of Routing Replay: simplification and full capacity utilization

outline.description: This chapter explores the practical benefits of GSPO for RL training infrastructure. It discusses the precision discrepancies between training and inference engines, explains why sequence-level likelihoods are more tolerant of these discrepancies than token-level likelihoods, and describes how GSPO enables direct use of inference engine likelihoods, simplifying infrastructure for scenarios like partial rollout and multi-turn RL.
subtopics: Precision discrepancies between training engines (e.g., Megatron) and inference engines (e.g., SGLang, vLLM)
Current practice: recomputing likelihoods with training engines
Why sequence-level likelihoods are more tolerant of precision discrepancies
Direct use of inference engine likelihoods in GSPO
Benefits for partial rollout scenarios
Benefits for multi-turn RL
Benefits for training-inference disaggregated frameworks
Potential for simplified RL infrastructure design

outline.description: This chapter summarizes the key contributions of GSPO, revisits its theoretical grounding in importance sampling principles, and discusses the broader implications for the future of large-scale RL training. It reflects on GSPO's role as a scalable algorithmic cornerstone and anticipates future advances in RL for language models.
subtopics: Summary of GSPO's key innovations: sequence-level importance ratios, clipping, and optimization
Theoretical grounding: alignment with the basic principle of importance sampling
Key empirical findings: stability, efficiency, and performance over GRPO
Resolution of MoE training stability challenges
Infrastructure simplification potential
GSPO as a scalable algorithmic foundation for continued RL scaling
Future directions: scaling RL with GSPO and anticipated advances in intelligence
